analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "Mr. Solicitor General. Mr. Chief Justice, may it please the court. The oral argument in these seven cases has thus far covered a wide range of new but very fundamental constitutional questions. In our view, none of them, or certainly almost none of them, need to be decided, and the United States takes no position upon them at this time, because we think that the convictions must be reversed upon narrower and much simpler grounds. I'd like first to lay to one side two of the cases, and then to come to the five with which the bulk of my argument will be concerned. First, we've filed no brief, and I shall not argue concerning right against Georgia, the case that was just argued for the court. The constitutional principles applicable to that case are well settled. It was conceded at the bar that discrimination on grounds of race in a city park was unconstitutional, and what is involved, therefore, is the application of fairly well-settled principles to particular facts. Second, I would like to deal briefly with Griffin against Maryland, the case involving the Glen Echo amusement park, because it seems to us that that case, too, can and should be decided upon grounds peculiar to it alone. The decisive facts, in our view, are three. First, Maryland delegated its police authority, a part of its sovereign power, to Lieutenant Collins, who was acting under the direction and control of the park, so that the park was, in every substantial sense, exercising the police power of Maryland. Second, Lieutenant Collins made the arrest and instituted the prosecution while on duty as a state officer. May I say in this connection that the warrants that appear at the beginning of the record, as I understand it, are warrants that serve the purpose of a complaint or information in many criminal proceedings. That is to say, this is the way the prosecution was started. And if you will look at the first, at the application for a warrant, you will see that the police officer recites in it that he had already made the arrest, so that this was not the initial step toward a formal arrest. He'd made the arrest, and this was the institution of the prosecution. In the Glen Echo case. In the Glen Echo case, yes. Third, admittedly, the park's instructions to Lieutenant Collins as to what he should do were based on grounds of race. Now, it seems to us that on those facts, the decisive propositions of law are also three. First, that when a state delegates its police power to a private person, the state is responsible, under the 14th Amendment, for the way that its police power is exercised. Why isn't that true also in the case of an ordinary police officer? The state is, because of my second proposition, I think is perhaps the best way to answer, Your Honor, we submit that the park manager's discriminatory motivation in ordering the petitioner to leave cannot be separated from his motivation in ordering the arrest and institution of the prosecution. In other words, you can't separate his mind into two compartments and say that when he asked the police officer to tell the petitioners to leave, yes, then he was acting out of a desire to promote segregation. But when he told the police officer to exercise the state's sovereign power, then he was acting in a non-discriminatory fashion. Just being in one man's mind, it's too close a connection, I suppose. Everstein David Brennan racistpress Hmm . wants to discriminate as here, because that's apparent in the record. Gets on the telephone and calls a policeman and says executed in a case where he hires this private detective who also has a badge. Doesn't it all add up to the same thing? Well, I think sometimes the fact that you can accomplish the same result in a constitutional way is not an excuse for going about it in an unconstitutional way. Now, when I say accomplish it in a constitutional way, let me make it plain that I am assuming that only for the purposes of argument. It was argued here, of course, a number of other grounds, and I don't mean to impliedly reject them at any point. I'm not dealing with it. But there are a good many things where the same result can be constitutionally accomplished. But nevertheless, if it is done unconstitutionally, there's a violation. Second, we think that here it is not clear that the same result would necessarily have followed. There is often a practical difference in dealing with minor crimes, squabbles between citizens, between what the police and how the police may act. They have a certain amount of discretion. I don't know about Glen Echo or City, but I do know in a small country town when two neighbors start rallying, the chief of police, if you think somebody is being unreasonable, he says, well, you'd better go and see the selectman Monday night. And then the selectmen don't have time for him that Monday night, and we tell him to come back at our next meeting a month later. There are many practical differences when the state exercises its own public discretion. One of the best illustrations in our history, of course, has been in connection with labor disputes. The conduct of deputized officers has been different over and over again from the conduct of formal public officers acting under the direction of public officials. Are you arguing, then, is it a deduction from your argument that if the state does exercise its discretion, the police officer comes in and makes the arrest? That's more state action or less state action than took place here? It is, in a sense, state action unquestionable. I would say that the question then became whether it was a state denial of equal protection of the laws. Here, I think, the state is responsible that the exercise of state power has been based on the discriminatory motive of the manager. In the case where the public official comes in separate, his motive may be that he is intervening for the purpose of supporting the private decision of the owner of the property to decide who he will license to appear upon it, regardless of the motive of the private person. But where it's a private person who is acting out of discriminatory motives and exercising the state power himself out of discriminatory motives, then it seems to me to be different. Now, in saying that, in stating the argument again, I didn't mean to reject the suggestion that it may be enough that the state arrests and prosecutes. The argument's been made based on Shelley and Kramer that it is. As to that, I simply take no position. But it seems to me distinctly different that I could concede that there was no state denial of equal protection of the laws where the superintendent of the police sends an officer to make the arrest and still make the argument I am here because the motives would be, or at least could be, entirely different. And here the motive, admittedly, the motive with which the manager acted was discriminatory. Wouldn't that be so in both cases? Yes, but the manager isn't exercising the state power in the case where the independent policeman comes and makes an independent judgment. But he is exercising the state power in this case. It's been given to him to exercise. In a sense, perhaps, it is fair to draw an analogy between this case and the case where the state gives its property, currently owned by it, as in Birmingham and Wilmington Parking Authority. And this court said that where the state gave its property in a state building to a lessee, then the state was involved to such an extent that it couldn't later pull back and say, oh, we have no responsibility. The private owner has made the decision. Well, so a forciera, if it gives its sovereign power, it can't later attempt to disentangle itself from the way that sovereign power is exercised. But isn't it entangled in both cases? Let's restate it. A private owner calls up the police and says, I don't want Negroes to come to Glen Echo. That's the basis of my decision. And therefore, since it is my decision that they should not come, I want you to make an arrest. And then the state comes and makes the arrest. How does that differ from a case where a private owner says, this is my decision, and I hire this man, and he has a badge to execute? In the second case, this man he has hired is his man, paid by him, hence with a duty of loyalty to him, following his direction, and exercising no independent judgment whatever. And regardless of what the answer may be, in the case where he has an opportunity to exercise some independent judgment, I submit that the state cannot disclaim the responsibility in the case where he has not. Now, it may well be, as has been suggested here, that there's enough state action in any of it. But in one case, it's a step removed. There has been an opportunity to make an independent judgment, to act on whatever grounds the state may care to act on. But one of those grounds, it's argued for the other side, is that we are going to act to protect owners to do as they please in admitting people to property. But where it's all in the same man's mind, I submit that he can't separate them out. I just think your argument could be run the other way. I mean, as you emphasize, this was a man paid by and exclusively under the control of the operator of Glen Echo, and not under the control of the state. But he's wielding state power. Well, in effect, Mr. Just like the man occupying the space in the Wilmington Parking Authority building was using state property. This man's wielding state power. What you're really saying is that we ought to consider the Glen Echo case as if that badge was worn by the manager of the park. Precisely. Precisely. Here. If, of course, the court rejects this ground, then in the Glen Echo case, other questions are presented. Now, I'd like Glen Echo to one side. And the Glen Echo case, in that case you cannot make, can you, the argument that you make in these city cases? No. Because Maryland does not have this massive group of segregation legislation. Nor any ordinance. Nor any ordinance. Nor any ordinance. Such as we rest on. No. I come now to the other five cases. And although there are strong arguments that have been made to the contrary, and which may turn out to be well-founded, I assume solely for the purposes of argument that the owners of stores, restaurants, and like establishments, do have the privilege of choosing their customers upon whatever grounds, however immoral or unworthy, and that a state does not violate the 14th Amendment by making its peace officers and courts available to all proprietors without discrimination and without scrutinizing the grounds of their decisions. As I say, I assume that simply for the purposes of argument, conscious that there are strong arguments on the other side, which may well prevail, and which would have to be considered if our ground is rejected. We think that the principle is not, that that principle that I assume is not applicable to these cases for two reasons. First, we are not dealing here in any substantial sense with the right of a property owner to choose whom he will admit and whom he will exclude. These stores were open to the general public in all five cases that I'm now speaking about, open to the general public without any discrimination. The owners solicited the patronage of Negroes, dealt with them regularly at all the other counters, and in several of the instances at least, the counters seemed to be all mixed up together, so that in anything except the most literal sense, Negroes were free to go anywhere in the store. But the only privilege that the proprietor is really asserting here is the privilege to subject Negroes to a social stigma of inferiority and to insist by preventing them from breaking bread together with white people. Now, from the standpoint of whether there is state responsibility, a state denial of equal protection, that fact may be unimportant. But if one comes to consider the other argument, that there are substantial private property rights involved in a constitutional sense, then it seems to us that Marsh in Alabama furnishes a complete answer and shows that there are no really substantial private property rights to be weighed in the scale here. The second difference, and more important difference, is that in these five cases, there was antecedent state action, which under well-settled principle, indeed indisputably violates the 14th of Methodist. He says so, Joe. Mr. Solicitor General. Mr. Chief Justice, may it please come on. I was just beginning to deal with the five remaining questions on the court rose for luncheon. Our basic view concerning them is that in each of these five cases, there was antecedent state action, which under well-settled principle, violates the Equal Protection Clause of the 14th Amendment. I refer, of course, to the ordinances in four of the cases, and in the fifth, the Louisiana case, there is a mass of current and pervasive state statutes establishing a state policy of racial segregation in all aspects of society. So it seems to us the only question here is whether the criminal convictions are so related to the unconstitutional state laws as to be invalid. And we think that they are. Basically, our proposition is that a state may not, consistently with the 14th Amendment, both induce the proprietors of businesses to engage in racial discrimination and then prosecute the victims for criminal trespass or some similar offense. Because of the importance of the ordinances, I would like to take just a minute to review the record with respect to them, beginning with Peterson against the city of Greenville. The Greenville ordinance is printed on page 35 of our brief, and it clearly required segregation in this Crest apartment store. It also happens, although we would make the same argument anyway, that the record does reveal the effect of the ordinance. Crest's manager testified that his instructions from the national organization were to adhere to local customs. Then when he was asked, Mr. West, why did you order your lunch hour closed? He replied, it's contrary to local customs, and it's also the ordinance that has been discussed. There's been some discussion of the... That ordinance means statute. Well, I don't see why anyone should read ordinance to mean statute. The distinction had been clearly drawn earlier in the trial, and ordinance to me on the face of it means ordinance. It is also plain that the ordinance was identified for the purposes of the record and was excluded only on the ground of the judge's substantive theory of law, which, of course, is challenged here. It also seems plain to me from the opinion of the appellant court that it regarded the ordinance as properly proved properly before it, but it thought that the ordinance was immaterial because it said the prosecution isn't founded on the ordinance, and therefore it's not before us. The second case, Gober against the city of Birmingham, the ordinance, the Birmingham ordinance, again one requiring segregation in these department stores at the eating place, is printed here in this case on page 22 of our breach. And again, the record shows that some attention was called to the effect of the ordinance. It was discussed at the trial. The trial card did cut off further inquiry, but we did get a certain amount of light into it. Thus the witness, Gutlinger, who was the controller of the store, testified in the Gober case that the assistant to the president, who was the one who asked Gober to leave, had said he told them that they couldn't be served here, and then later he told them that it would be against the law to serve them here. This was the reason given by the store in the Gober case to require them to leave. The point was certainly raised in the trial court by the petitioners. Counsel explained, it's our theory of this case that it is one based simply upon the city's segregation officer, and Mr. Gottlinger, the controller, Mr. Pizzitz, the assistant to the president of the store, and the police officers and everyone, acted simply because of the segregation law. So we submit that so far as the trial court is concerned, there is no question about this having been brought out in the lead case. It was adverted to in a second of these cases, all that were in another of these cases that were tried in sequence at record 166 and 168, and I think the circumstances of the hearing makes it plain in substance that what was the judge was the same judge, what he'd been given notice of in one case, but he clearly had notice of in the other. Now it's been argued that Alabama has some rules of procedure that prevent taking this ordinance into account. I don't feel qualified to discuss Alabama procedure in any detail, and I think I will have to leave that to the arguments of counsel who are more familiar with it, but there are a few points that I think I should note that may be helpful to the court. One is that the cases cited for the proposition that these prosecutions are governed by the rules of civil practice and seem to have to do only with the assignment of errors on appeal, and none of those cases, I can't speak as to the understanding of the Alabama Bar, but none of those cases, as we read them, have anything to do with the filing of special pleas in the trial court or replications or other forms of pleading. Second, it's entirely clear that the Alabama statute not only permits, but apparently requires the court to take judicial notice of this ordinance. Third, it appears not to be disputed that the petitioners in these cases did properly argue to the Alabama appellate courts the proposition that they were being denied the equal protection of the laws in the violation of the 14th Amendment. Now, it seems to me that the reference to the segregation ordinance under these circumstances is the kind of legal reasoning that a lawyer develops under that main point that it's subordinate to it, a specific application of it, rather than the kind of point that you would ordinarily be required to raise separately. And again, although we certainly haven't exhausted the matter of research, looking in the obvious places, we find no Alabama case that would seem to prevent the argument having been raised in that fashion. There may be some that aren't as obvious that one would look at in the course of an afternoon. So that we think that it cannot be assumed, and indeed would be contrary to a general experience, that the Alabama court couldn't have taken note of this argument. What was argued to it, of course, I don't know. I don't know whether anything was said to the Alabama. The brief wasn't available in Washington, and we don't know what was said to the Alabama. Or whether the ordinance was pointed out to them. What? You don't know whether the ordinance was pointed out to them? We know from the opinion that the court said the ordinance is irrelevant, as I read it, because the case wasn't founded on the ordinance. There's no charge that they violated the ordinance. Now, the language is a little broader. It says there's no pleading. It's not based on the Gopar case. The Gopar case. The language of the opinion is a little broader. It says there's no pleading based on the ordinance. But reading it in context, the impression I get, it can't be more than that, one can't say with assurance, is that they were saying, as the South Carolina court did, that this isn't a prosecution on the ordinance, so stop talking about the ordinance. Well, that isn't, as I shall attempt to show a little later, a complete answer. Now, Shuttlesworth, of course, is governed by the same considerations in this respect as Gopar. The charge was that Shuttlesworth either incited or aided and abetted in a violation of the criminal trespass statute. The same ordinance, same segregation ordinance, is involved, and it has the same pertinence as before. If what he was advising these young people to do was constitutionally protected under the circumstances, then, of course, he committed no crime in advising them to do it. The fourth case is a event against North Carolina. We've set forth, on page six of our brief, the ordinance of the city of Durham. Now, in this case, it is quite clear that the ordinance was not mentioned in the trial court, and apparently it was not mentioned on appeal. It is also clear that the North Carolina courts will not ordinarily take judicial notice of a municipal ordinance. The North Carolina statutes do set forth specific ways of proving an ordinance. The reference, if the court is concerned, is GS 160-272, or alternatively, GS 8-5. At this bar, yesterday, or the day before, it was stated by council that the ordinance we have printed here is an ordinance of the city of Durham, that the ordinance is still in effect in the city of Durham, and that it has been marked to be repealed. Now, under those circumstances, the only ground, the doubt as to the existence of the ordinance or as to the correctness of the reported form as to its not having been amended or repealed, is entirely removed. And the use... It was conceded that it was unconstitutional, as indeed it undoubtedly is. I don't think that removes, for reasons I'll tell you, to date a little later, its significance from this case. It also is the rule that where councils stipulate as to an ordinance, then the normal objection to judicial notice is removed. This, the authority that I can refer the court to, is a Tennessee case, Gidey against the city of Memphis, 263 Southwestern, 532 at 535. Now, did you make the statement by the gospel and the situation by this person? Is this situation worth it forever? I would think it was regarded as an it was an acknowledgment of its existence and that it was correctly set forth here. But yes, if I made such a statement, I would expect to be held by and I assume that he did. Also, I'm not trying to trap him into anything. Oh, I don't think there's any stipulation as to its effect on the case. If I said that, I quite misstate it, misspoke myself. That it exists. And so, yes, and therefore the necessity of proving it I would say was removed. Now, there's a question that remains whether as a matter of what I was going to say remains, perhaps we'll answer, Your Honor. I was going to say the question remains whether it can be brought up this late. But that would be not the normal obstacle to taking judicial notice, but a state ground having to do with raising at this stage something this far along. As to that, I'd suggest two things. First, we are assuming that the ordinance is considered in the South Carolina case, as it must be, and that this court should hold, as I shall argue when I get to the substance, that the North Carolina conviction must be reversed because of it. Then we would have it established, substantive constitutional law, that in the Durham case there was a deprivation of constitutional rights in the conviction. Now, I find it very hard to believe, Mr. Justice Goldberg, that if the matter came before the North Carolina court in that posture with an admission that the ordinance did exist, that it would still say, well, it's too bad, and the petitioners must go to jail, even though this deprives them of their constitutional rights, because they didn't foresee what the Supreme Court would ultimately hold. And I think that this court, it would seem to me, has the same power to do what it thinks the North Carolina court would do, and that is take the ordinance into account. I would also point out that in the Turman-Yellow case, the court did decide it and reverse unconstitutional grounds because of an error in the charge that had not been raised in the state courts. Finally, and perhaps most important, this court, under the relevant section of the judicial code, 28 U.S.C. 2106, is of course not limited to affirming, modifying, or reversing, but it may make such disposition of a case as justice may require. Now here, not only would we have this supervening event showing that a event had been denied his constitutional rights, but the court would also have in front of it some other constitutional issues that seem to us to be new and far-reaching, which may someday have to be decided, but which don't have to be decided now. And under these grounds, justice would seem plainly to require, if this court can't notice the ordinance, sending the case back to the North Carolina court in order to give it an opportunity to deal with these supervening events. And I think I have a clear precedent for that proposition. In Patterson against Alabama, which unfortunately I neglected to cite it by brief, in Patterson against Alabama, 294 U.S., 600, and I've got a quote from 606 as the court will come in. In Patterson against Alabama, there was a conviction in the Alabama courts, and the defendant sought to raise in this court a constitutional claim. He had not properly preserved his point in the Alabama courts, court, according to state law. At the same time, the Patterson case was before the court. Another case, Norris, was before the court, which involved the same constitutional issue, properly raised. The court sustained the constitutional claim in Norris, and then the question was, what should it do with Patterson? The court held that it would remand Patterson to the Alabama court in the light of these supervening events. And the court said we've frequently held that in the exercise of our appellate jurisdiction, we've power not only to correct error in the judgment under review, but to make such disposition of the case as justice may require. And then it went on and explained much that I have just said, and sent the case back to the Alabama court to see whether their procedure wouldn't permit them to deal with this new development. Now there is one difference. In that case, it was a capital offense. In this case, it's going to jail in deprivation of your proper constitutional right. Thirty days is obviously not as irremediable as execution. Otherwise, it seems to me the cases are on all fours. The Patterson case was followed in this court in Williams against Georgia, 349 U.S. 375, 349 U.S. 375, where Justice Franks would are quoted from the passage to which I have just referred to the court. Can we send the case back to the rule? Two points. North Carolina court to change the rule on judicial law? No, I don't think you would be telling the North Carolina court to do anything if the North Carolina court should refuse to take these supervening events into account. Why, then, perhaps there would be another ground for bringing the case here, and there certainly would be the grounds that counsel have argued that we do not press. But what just the position, Mr. Justice Goldberg, would be that justice requires giving the North Carolina court a chance to decide what it would do under North Carolina procedure in the light of these events. In this case, there's a very good reason for doing it. It would be the application of the old, of the familiar rule that the court should not rush to decide novel and unnecessary constitutional questions. And by hypothesis, on my argument, in the South Carolina case, you would have decided one constitutional question, so you wouldn't be adding to excuse me, Justice Stokes. Am I right in recollecting that in Williams against Georgia, this gambit wasn't received very hospitably by the state of Georgia? I confess I haven't. Perhaps we may expect better of North Carolina. It seems to me that's not a reason not to give North Carolina the chance, whatever the upshot may be. Or not to give the petitioners the chance, whatever the upshot may be. Assuming that one or all of these courses are open, what bearing do you think it has that the record shows that, in this case at least, this restaurateur was operating in violation of the statute, namely operating the integrated stand-up restaurant? Well, I think that that is not sufficient to... Two points. First, I think that's not sufficient to overcome the considerations that I am now going on to develop. And I think if I might come back to your question, if I haven't answered it in developing them, I'd be happy to do so. Second, it seems to me that there is a question as to whether the ordinance was understood to apply to stand-up places. It was said at the bar here, the argument of earlier cases by people who know the customs better than I do, that these things apply to sitting down together, that they don't apply to standing up together. Well, in that event, the ordinance may have carried just as much force with respect to sitting down as if there had been no acquiescence in a violation with respect to standing up. An analogy, I don't suggest compelling, but to show what I'm trying to say, there are many places where it's well known that the speed law is 50 miles an hour, but that as long as you don't drive over 55, nobody will arrest you. And this may be true in the application of that ordinance. Now, that isn't my only answer, and I go on to say now why we think the ordinances are decisive in these cases. The first three steps in my reasoning seem to me to be clear beyond the dispute. The first is that an ordinance requiring racial segregation is, of course, unconstitutional. Second, I take it that it's agreed on all sides that if petitioners had been prosecuted for violating the ordinances or for procuring and aiding and abetting violations, that that conviction would have to be set aside as a violation of the 14th Amendment because a denial of equal protection of the law. And third, if a state, by injunction or active threats of prosecution, required a department store unwillingly to expel Negroes from a lunch counter where whites were being served, and then the Negroes were prosecuted for criminal trespass for failing to leave, surely that their convictions would be set aside as the results of a denial of equal protection of the law. The state can't insulate itself from responsibility for unconstitutional state discrimination by requiring some private person to do its dirty work for it, if I may put it colloquially. That's been adjudicated in a number of lower court decisions cited in our brief, and I take it that this proposition, too, no one would dispute here. So the question would seem to come down to this. Can the states defend these convictions as colorblind in the face of ordinances requiring the segregation based upon color upon the ground that the ordinances and the convictions are separated by the owner's decision to segregate? which decision may or may not have been the result of the order? We think that even if that is an accurate statement of the fact, that the link between the ordinance and the conviction is still too close, and that the conviction must be set aside upon such a record as a denial, as the result of a denial of equal protection of the law. Mr. Schlister, General, I think you began your argument by making the assumption, which you just said was an assumption, that there was nothing in the Constitution that would forbid an owner of a private restaurant from selecting his clientele, even though his selection was based on a mischievous or immoral or, you or I might think, prejudiced and wrong set of criteria. But wouldn't your present argument mean that a, if there were, if, if, that a restaurateur in one of these southern states which has segregation statutes and, let's say, a specific segregation, restaurant segregation ordinance, wouldn't this prevent, wouldn't this prevent the proprietor of a restaurant from selecting his clientele on a racial basis, even though he, in his prejudice way, wanted to do that? I think not for several reasons. Let me state them now. They, again, may become clearer after I've said a few intermediate things, but the reasons are these. First, it seems to me that in these cases, it is not necessary for us to go beyond the point of saying that if the decision is based upon the desire of the owner of premises without regard to the command or inducement of the state, that the burden of proving that rests upon the state, if it's a criminal prosecution, and upon the owner if he is bringing a private action. And that in these cases, the inference and the presumption are the other way, and that there is not only nothing to overcome them, but certainly in the South Carolina case, and in the Gober case in Alabama, there's a great deal of the contrary. Well, I say that in these cases, it is enough to say that the state hasn't overcome the presumption. Now, we have gone beyond that in the brief, and I'm quite prepared to go beyond. I'm prepared to say that where a state has such an ordinance, that the state cannot both command people to segregate, and at the same time come into court and defend the prosecution for criminal conviction on the ground that its command had nothing to do with the owner's decision. In other words, if we had to, we would be prepared to take that next step. Well, this would mean... We don't think it has to be taken here. This would mean that a man running a restaurant in Montana could exclude all Negroes and serve white people only, but a man running a restaurant in South Carolina could not. Well, I think again, no, because I think again, the upshot in a prosecution by the state need not be the same as the upshot in a case brought by the private owner. That is, the parallel does not have to follow. Now let me... Well, might I, before... I haven't done any more than make an assertion to Justice Stewart. I haven't given any reason. Might I first ask Cleve to state my reasons for the presumption and our reasons for saying that the ordinance would bind the state, and then against that background, it is easier to say how far they would or would not be applicable where the private owner was setting up his right. I don't want to run away from it, but I think it would be a great good clearer if I did it that way. Now we say essentially that there are three reasons for concluding in the absence of any other showing. That where the state has such a command, it has significantly intruded itself, it has significantly involved itself, in Justice Clark's phrase, in the Wilmington Parking Authority case, in the discrimination. I would emphasize as a predicate that it's entirely clear on the decisions that if the state is a substantial influence in bringing about the discrimination, it doesn't exculpate it on the ground that there has been some opportunity for private decision in between. That is the Wilmington Parking Authority case. It's Derrington and Plumont. That's the other cases dealing with restaurants at city facilities of one kind or another. Well, isn't it always such if it sends people to jail for doing what has been done here? Well, I think that it is always state action. I think the question is whether it is always a state denial of equal protection. And the answer to that might be yes for the reasons that counsel have argued, or it might be otherwise, as was argued for the other side. I am assuming, for the purposes of our discussion, that the mayor sending of people to jail for trespassing is not a state denial of equal protection of the laws. That may be a false assumption. I don't want to embrace it permanently. Now, here we think there are three strong reasons for concluding that the state was sufficiently involved. In the first place, when a state orders people to segregate their restaurants, the normal factual inferences, that that law simply has an influence on the action of proprietors. For one thing, having been told to do it, they have no occasion to consider what they might otherwise wish to do. Or perhaps more realistically, in terms of some of these communities, if they might fall away from the local custom, they have no opportunity to do it, because the ordinance takes away from them the power and the responsibility of a private decision. In the Peterson case, as I pointed out, the manager said, it's the local custom, it's also the ordinance that's been discussed. Now, a second factor, certainly, is that department stores, situated as these are, don't ordinarily act by themselves. And the matters of this kind, the leading stores, will follow a common practice. And therefore, even if one particular store didn't know anything about the ordinance, it still would be likely that other stores did know about it, that they were influenced in their decision that way, and that this had its impact upon the particular man who said, I never heard of the ordinance. Third, I would emphasize, again, in support of this basic factual inference, that true freedom of private choice carries commercial and moral consequences that are affected by an ordinance dictating the decision. Here, as I pointed out earlier, these stores were opened to Negroes and solicited their patron. Now, it's one thing to serve them food, saying, I won't do it. It's another thing to say, as I said in Pizzit's store, the law won't let me do it. Not only are the commercial consequences likely to be different, but indeed the moral problem that the man faces in making that decision is entirely different. And I think it's a misnomer to describe a decision made under such an ordinance as a free private choice. Second, in support of the proposition that the states are involved, we invoke the familiar principle with the wide application in the law, that where one does a wrong, as learned hand once put it, the burden is on him to disentangle the consequences for which he is chargeable from those which he can show he had no relation to, or else bear the consequences for the whole. And so here, the states having unquestionably violated the constitutional rights of Negroes, including the petitioners, it is up to the state to prove that its unquestionable violation had no relation to the owner's decisions and still to these convictions. The court, do you draw any distinction in that respect in an ordinance that was passed before Brown against the board when, with the approval of this court, what was being done was being done, and one that was passed since? I doubt that I would draw any significant distinction. I think in these cases, unless perhaps it were shown, and I underscore that perhaps, unless perhaps it were shown that the ordinance were one widely ignored by everyone concerned, or one which had possibly been the subject of a specific court decree in that community. But we all know that the decision in Brown has not been made to take effect in a large number of places on the local authority, and that in many places they wait until there's been an injunction or even a threat of contempt. In other words, they don't. But I think a department store owner in a particular community would assume, and we are entitled to assume, that the ordinance is a living thing, at least until the contrary is shown. Now there's one other point. I'm wondering if, perhaps you haven't got this through, perhaps you don't care to take position, but I was wondering if the Department of Justice thought that a institution of segregation could be perpetuated through this freedom of choice conception of the sacrosanct private property, whether it be a bus company owned by stockholders or a retail store owned by one man or a chain store owned by a big group. Well, I think that the question your Honor is raising is one which may someday be raised in these cases. At that time we no doubt will take a position upon it. But it is not one that we feel and encumbered upon us to take a position on now, because it doesn't require a decision at this time. And our failing to do so isn't intended to express anything but the familiar rule of deciding the case. … I think there is a difference between customs supported by the state's command and customs without the state's command. As to what the rule would be if we had a case of customs without the state's command, as to that, I don't think it's necessary for the court to make a decision. It is certainly arguable that customs of a number of people is something different from the individual choice of people acting alone. But it also seems to me that it is certainly arguable that custom resulting from the private action of a lot of people may be something different from the action of the state. The whole foundation of your argument could be brushed right away if the states went through the motions of repealing all these segregation ordinances and statutes. I don't think that's a significant consequence, Your Honor. Now, if I've answered that, I don't want to sit down. I see that my time has almost expired. I don't want to sit down without directing myself to the question that you raised earlier. It's very important. And that is, well, isn't the effect of your argument to say that private citizens in the city of Greenville no longer have the right to choose their customs? My answers are these. First, that no rule may be laid down here that goes beyond saying that until the fact is proved that a man made the choice without regard to the ordinance, the convictions must be set aside as the result of significant state involvement, not state compulsion, significant state involvement in the outcome. Second, the presumption that I invoked about disentangling consequences would work somewhat differently when a private person was active. And third, because it runs against the wrongdoer. It wouldn't run against the private person. Then you are proposing a separate rule for the South and another one for Montana. I'm suggesting a rule for any place that has such an ordinance and not for anybody else. You're talking about custom. No, I think not, Mr. Justice. I think I disclaimed associating myself with Justice Goldberg's view just to lay it one's son and what I say is applicable to any place that has an ordinance. Now, I see no reason, Mr. Justice Stewart, that the upshot where the private owner asserts his right must be just the same as where the state acts. And to take a rather foolish illustration, but one which may make the meaning clear, if I, if a Negro in the South, were to steal your automobile and were to be indicted before a grand jury, or the, what do you call it, for which was excluded Negroes, the call for the grand jury. Systematic exclusion. Systematic exclusion of Negroes. Then, so long as that persisted, the man who stole the car could not validly be convicted of crime. But I take it that you would have the right to sue him for trespass. And you could get your car back. And equally here, I take it, that anything we have said by a parity of reasoning would not require a result that would hold that the Negroes have a right to compel these store owners to open up. Now, maybe they do, or maybe they don't. I would add one qualification, and that is if it is quite clear on the decisions in the Fourth and Fifth Circuits that if the owner excludes them on the basis of the ordinance, then he is acting under color of state law. And under the present Civil Rights Act, of course, an action would lie against him. In the Louisiana case, Chief Justice Warren, we submit that the mass of current and pervasive state laws, and I emphasize current laws, enacted as recently as 1960, detailing the policy of Louisiana in favor of segregation, play exactly the same role that the ordinances do under the argument that I've just presented. Since the Solicitor General, both in his brief and in an oral argument, agrees, at least by assumption, with the basic postulate that we have submitted in our case, that a private businessman, regardless of whether or not his motives are praiseworthy or commendable, may nevertheless deal with those individuals or persons whom he chooses, the case against Maryland, as the Solicitor General has stated, is that Maryland, through some old statute, had delegated its police power to the private businessman and, therefore, the power of the state and the power of the private businessman have been merged and that, therefore, this is state action. That is not the police officer's duty. That is the magistrate's duty to determine who is right and wrong in this controversy. And a police officer who would take it upon himself to be the judge is acting way beyond the scope of his authority. It's not every day. Well, of course it is, Your Honor. Minor offenses, like if there's no money for lawyers and generally conduct. And if she insists that a charge be placed against me, it's the duty of the officer to take me to the police station and see that I'm charged, not for him to make the decision. It is normally the practice in such cases for the officer to say to your wife, you arrest him and I'll take him to the police station. And then he takes him to the police station and then you go through your proceeding. But this didn't happen within his practice. But the practice is, and it happens many times, that both the husband and wife would go to the police station and the warrant would be sworn out at that time. But if your Honor plays here also, why I also raise the point that there might be a difference without a distinction here, I think as Mr. Justice Goldberg tried to bring out with the Solicitor General, is that the police officer Collins here, the special deputy sheriff, could have gone down and sworn out what we generally know as a show-cause order, as a subpoena to appear before the magistrate to show cause why he shouldn't be charged. It buttresses up private ownership.
